title: Fragment brokering and verified backfill reconnect protocol
creator: Ava Chen
description: Problem: current SSE reconnect behavior relies on resume tokens embedded in the stream with minimal validation. For long-running responses with interleaved function/tool calls and structured JSON fragments we see partial-output duplication or loss during reconnects and replays. Goal: implement a fragment brokering layer and a verified backfill protocol so clients can reliably resume without duplicating tool/function-call side effects and without large latency regressions for normal traffic.
background_and_context: Existing tickets have focused on framing, resume tokens, and windowed checkpoints but assume resume semantics are purely client-driven. We need a brokered approach to centralize short-lived checkpoints at the edge and provide a deterministic replay path for late-arriving fragments.

Target users: Redwood hosted API customers using streaming chat/gen with tool/function calls and structured output (JSONL/ODDS). This aims to reduce customer-visible duplicate function calls and improve rejoin success rate under flaky mobile networks.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Clients that reconnect with a valid resume token can be resumed without duplicated function/tool side effects for >=95% of disconnect scenarios in the integration test harness.
2) End-to-end latency for non-reconnect streams increases by <3% at p95 when the broker is enabled compared to the legacy path.
3) SDK-level connectors (JS/node, Python, and browser polyfill) can negotiate the new protocol and fall back to legacy SSE when the server indicates unsupported.
4) Observability: per-stream metrics emitted for broker hit/miss, backfill bytes, and replayed-fragment-count. Dashboards created in the console-2025.03 release.
5) No customer-visible double-execution of function/tool calls observed in canary traffic (0 incidents during 1 week of 10% traffic).
decisions: Use a lightweight 'checkpoint broker' service colocated on edge nodes to hold ephemeral fragment checkpoints for N seconds (configurable, default 45s).

Frame format will extend our JSONL framing with a small binary header for monotonic frame_id (64-bit hex), seq_offset, semantic_hint (enum: TEXT_BOUNDARY | TOOL_CALL_BOUNDARY | JSON_STRUCT_BOUNDARY), and sha256 digest of the payload. Digest helps clients verify integrity during backfill.

Reconnect negotiation: clients send last_ack_frame and optional last_seen_toolcall_id. Server/broker returns a backfill bundle (zero or more frames) plus an authoritative next_resume_token. If the toolcall ID in the backfill conflicts with server executed toolcalls, server will rewrite backfill into an abbreviated 'suppress' token indicating the client must request a delta fetch rather than re-execute.
Prefer server-side suppression of duplicate toolcalls over client-side optimistic dedupe. This keeps functioncall idempotency decisions centralized and reduces SDK complexity.

Transport compatibility: still use text/event-stream content-type for SSE. The server will advertise protocol version via an initial :meta comment line (e.g., ':rdi-p:1'). Clients that do not understand the meta header will fall back to legacy streaming behavior.
tradeoffs: Pros: Centralized broker reduces likelihood of duplicate side effects and gives precise backfill, improving UX on flaky connections.
Cons: Added operational component (broker) increases surface area and latency for cold streams. We'll mitigate with edge-local brokers and in-memory caches with TTL.
Complexity: Frame digests and semantic hints require changes across runtime, SDKs, and language bindings. However, the metadata payload is small and designed to be backwards compatible.
Security: persisted checkpoints contain partial response payloads; TTL and encryption at rest required. We'll integrate broker with existing KMS and RBAC for access control.
implementation_notes: Server-side runtime changes: emit frames with 16-byte header: {frame_id(uint64), seq_offset(uint32), semantic_hint(uint8), flags(uint8)} followed by payload and sha256 trailer. The runtime will compute digest and attach as a trailing ':digest' property in the JSONL boundary.

Broker service: edge process exposes HTTP API /v1/checkpoint/{stream_id} to store and fetch backfill bundles. Backfill bundles are limited to 64KB by default and expire after TTL. Broker will verify digest against stored fragments before returning to clients.

Reconnect flow: client reconnects -> server checks resume_token -> if server has brokered fragments return them immediately as a single SSE event type 'backfill' containing base64-encoded bundle; client SDK consumes and validates digests, applies fragments in order.

Toolcall idempotency: runtime will tag function call frames with a stable toolcall_id. If a replay would re-run a toolcall the runtime will mark the backfill frame as 'suppress' and will include a mapping that allows SDKs to request result-only updates instead of re-execution.

Compatibility shim: legacy clients will receive plain framed JSONL lines without the meta header/digest and will still be able to reconnect using old resume tokens. We'll incrementally roll out by feature flag.
test_plan: Unit tests: header encoding/decoding, digest verification, broker TTL eviction, suppression mapping logic.
Integration: end-to-end harness simulating mobile reconnect patterns (random disconnects, packet loss, reorder) validating no duplicate toolcalls and that final assembled output matches baseline.
Chaos tests: large-scale disconnect storms against canary edge with broker enabled to validate resource limits and graceful degradation (broker returns 'too_big' or 'no_backfill' markers).
Performance: benchmark p50/p95 latency of stream start and of reconnect path with backfill sizes 1KB, 8KB, 64KB. Goal: <3% regression for non-reconnect flows.
SDK tests: JS/node, Python, browser—validate fallback to legacy SSE when server advertises unsupported protocol.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (dev): implement runtime framing and broker in dev environment behind feature flag. Unit + integration tests pass.
Phase 2 (canary): enable for 10% of hosted API streams on a subset of regions (us-west-2, eu-west-1). Monitor metrics: broker_hit_rate, backfill_bytes, replayed_toolcalls_count, stream_latency_p95.
Phase 3 (expand): increase to 50% if canary stable for 72h; add Dedicated customer opt-in.
Phase 4 (GA): enable by default; provide console toggle per-customer to disable broker for compliance-sensitive customers.
Rollback: server responds with 'legacy' header and broker TTL=0 to revert clients to legacy behavior immediately.
observability_and_telemetry: Emit per-stream metrics: broker_store_latency_ms, broker_fetch_latency_ms, backfill_size_bytes, backfill_returned_count, suppress_mappings_count.
Structured logs for backfill decisions with sampling for 1% of requests. Correlate with request_id and resume_token.
Console dashboards: streaming/backfill overview, per-region error heatmap, SDK-fallback rates.
security_and_compliance: Broker stores ephemeral payloads for a short TTL; ensure encryption at rest and access control via service identity.
Resume tokens include HMAC with server secret and TTL to prevent arbitrary resume requests.
For Private deployments: broker runs inside VPC as an optional component; default TTL reduced and admin can disable broker completely.
